title: TailHedge flush policy exploratory notes
content:
Status: exploratory draft - notes, traces, and a small matrix of runs.

Summary:
This doc captures an experimental idea and early run notes for a "TailHedge" flush policy: a hybrid flush mechanism that attempts hedged/timed flushes for long-waiting slots while preserving batching fairness. The goal is to reduce p99/p999 tail latency for latency-sensitive tenants without catastrophically increasing token cost or starving throughput-oriented tenants.

Motivation / Observed problem:
- Continuous batching currently trades latency for throughput. Long timeouts improve throughput but create large 99.9th-percentile latencies when requests straggle.
- Existing timeout-based flush + prefill rules help but we observed recurring ~3-8x p99 spikes during microbursts in production (see linked traces).
- We want a lightweight policy that: 1) triggers occasional hedged flushes for a small fraction of very-old requests; 2) avoids flushing whole queues and keeps most of the batching economics; 3) integrates with per-tenant fairness quotas.

TailHedge idea (high level):
- Track per-slot "age" histogram in the queue.
- When a request crosses an upper age threshold T_h (e.g. 80ms), schedule a hedged flush event after jitter J drawn from an exponential with mean m_j.
- The hedged flush will flush only the aged requests (slot-level) or a small capped window (N_hedge tokens) rather than entire batch.
- Hedge activation is rate-limited per-tenant (max H hedges / sec) to control cost.
- If an aged request is served in the meantime (prefill, probe), cancel the hedge.

Hypotheses:
1) TailHedge will reduce p99/p999 by absorbing the longest-waiting requests without breaking big-batch throughput for the median.
2) If H is too high or m_j too small, we will significantly reduce batching efficiency and increase avg token cost.
3) Proper per-tenant budgeting prevents noisy neighbors from exploiting hedges.

Experiment matrix (initial):
- baseline: current soft-timeout flush = 120ms, prefill enabled, no hedges.
- run A: T_h=80ms, m_j=10ms, J uniform jitter +-5ms, H=1/sec per tenant, N_hedge=4 requests
- run B: T_h=60ms, m_j=5ms, H=2/sec, N_hedge=8
- run C: T_h=100ms, m_j=20ms, H=0.5/sec, N_hedge=2
- run D: T_h=80ms, m_j=10ms, H=1/sec, N_hedge=4, fairness=aggressive (priority demotion if tenant uses >75% hedges)

Instrumentation to collect:
- Standard quantiles: p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 per route and per-tenant.
- Batch size distribution pre- and post-flush (histogram).
- Per-flush cost delta: estimate tokens generated vs baseline (we approximate cost by average token-per-request historically).
- Microtrace capture: when a hedge executes annotate the trace with hedge_id, slot_ages, kernel-run-id, GPU occupancy snapshot.
- NVTX and runtime counters for kernel hotspots during hedged flushes (we want to detect small-batch kernel inefficiencies).
- Queue-level metrics: #hedges fired, hedges cancelled, hedges that resulted in single-request small batches.

Small-run results (staging cluster replay of 2h production trace):
- Baseline: p50=22ms p95=48ms p99=210ms p999=540ms, mean batch size=7.3
- Run A: p50=23ms p95=45ms p99=120ms p999=260ms, mean batch size=6.1, hedges fired=430, cancelled=110, avg hedge-batch-size=3.2
- Run B: p50=24ms p95=49ms p99=98ms p999=220ms, mean batch size=5.6, hedges fired=830, cancelled=90, avg hedge-batch-size=4.8
- Run C: p50=22ms p95=47ms p99=180ms p999=420ms, mean batch size=6.9, hedges fired=210, cancelled=70, avg hedge-batch-size=2.0
- Run D (fairness demotion): p50=23ms p95=46ms p99=115ms p999=240ms, mean batch size=5.9, hedges fired=410, demotions=12, demotion_duration_mean=4.2s

Early interpretation notes:
- TailHedge reduces tail (p99/p999) substantially in A/B/D at the cost of reduced mean batch size. The biggest delta is between baseline and B for p99 (~112ms reduction).
- Run B used more hedges and had best tail improvement, but mean batch size dropped the most => throughput cost. Need to measure end-to-end token cost impact on real workloads.
- Run C (large T_h) shows fewer hedges and less improvement; suggests threshold tuning is critical.
- Demotion scheme (D) seems to keep tenants fairly bounded while preserving much of the tail improvement. Worth refining demotion thresholds and hysteresis.

Profiling observations (microtraces / kernel):
- Hedged flushes frequently create small batches that trigger less efficient kernel paths (we saw up to 1.5x per-token GPU time for batch sizes <=4 on GPU_A100_40GB with the current kernel selection).
- NVTX shows that small-batch `softmax` and `attention` kernels have lower occupancy and higher per-token latency. Consider adding a small-batch optimized kernel or fuse softmax+dropout path for these cases.
- Memory copy overhead is non-trivial for many small-batch hedges; batching fewer but larger hedges preferred over many single-request hedges.

Open questions / risks:
- Cost: how to present hedges in billing? If hedges increase per-token compute, customers may object. Need pricing guidance or automatic cost guardrails.
- Attack surface: could a tenant artificially create many near-threshold requests to force hedges and waste capacity? The per-tenant H rate-limit + demotion should help but needs solid tests.
- Kernel work: are there quick wins in kernel selection to reduce small-batch overhead? Might be faster to tune allocator and reduce memcpy overheads.
- SLO interactions: how do hedges interact with existing rollout fallbacks (model-variant fallback)? Hedge could cause two variants to execute concurrently unless we block it.

Next steps / TODOs:
- [ ] Add a histogram of per-tenant hedge usage to the console dashboard (short term telemetry). (owner: Jonah)
- [ ] Run cost-simulations: combine token cost delta with hedges to estimate per-tenant monthly cost impact (owner: Luis).
- [ ] Implement a soft throttle that blocks hedges if GPU occupancy < threshold (experiment 2).
- [ ] Prototype small-batch kernel/fusion micro-PR (paired with research team) to reduce the 1.5x penalty.
- [ ] Replay longer traces (24h) across a wider mix of routes with Run B params but H rate-limit lowered.
- [ ] Draft a short RFC for hedged flushes including billing/guardrail suggestions.

Notes-to-self / experimental artifacts:
- Replay harness: serving/tools/replay/trace_replayer_v2 -- use branch trace-replay-tailhedge.
- Quick grep: grep -n "hedge" serving/scheduler | head -n 40 to find current experimental hooks.
- Slack thread: <#runtime-batching> thread ts=1709752321 for raw field observations.
- Kernel perf snapshots saved to s3://redwood-staging/perf/tailhedge/2025-11-06/

Appendix: small sanity checks and heuristics tried but not included above:
- Limit hedges to only requests with <=R tokens remaining in average expectation — reduces useless hedges for long-generation jobs. This helped for conversational routes.
- Hedge-backoff: if hedges fire and cancel repeatedly for the same tenant, back off the tenant's H rate-limit adaptively.
- Probing variant: Instead of flushing immediately, send a tiny probe (empty prefix) to check if backend can pick up the request sooner — complicated and probably not worth it.

Unresolved decisions:
- Billing model: "count hedges as normal tokens" vs "apply a small surcharge for hedge overhead". Legal/Finance input needed.
- UI surface: should Console show hedge events per invocation? maybe aggregated per-hour.

If anyone wants to run additional quick probes against staging, ping me (Aisha). Will follow up with PR linking the initial impl and a short recorded trace walkthrough.

-- Aisha

(rough, intentionally choppy; this doc is a working area for the team, move to RFC once we converge)
